finding.claim: Mass assignment on PUT /me. The whole request body is merged into the authenticated user object and saved, so any user can set privileged fields on their own record (e.g. role, isAdmin, tenantId, id, email-verified flags). The sibling handler PUT /me/profile destructures only displayName and bio, which shows the allowlist was intended. Object.assign also copies an own '__proto__' key from JSON.parse output, but that only sets the target's prototype and does not pollute Object.prototype.
finding.source: req.body (JSON) of PUT /me, controlled by any authenticated low-privilege user
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) followed by req.store.save(req.user) persists the attacker-chosen fields and returns them

trace.note: PUT /me handler takes req.body with no schema validation
Object.assign copies every body key onto req.user, with no field allowlist
The modified user is persisted via req.store.save
The modified user is echoed back in the response

finding.guards_checked: No allowlist, no schema validation and no readonly-field filter in this file. The PUT /me/profile sibling at line 11 does destructure displayName and bio, so that one is SAFE. The auth middleware that sets req.user is not in this directory (only users.js exists), so whether it is applied was not verifiable. The finding assumes req.user is a normal authenticated user, as the handler implies.

verdict.reason: users.js:5 runs Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no allowlist or schema check, then users.js:6 saves it and users.js:7 returns it, while the sibling handler at users.js:11 destructures only displayName and bio. The auth middleware isn't in this directory, but the handler assumes an authenticated low-privilege user, so any such user can set privileged fields on their own record.
